title: Apocock
summary: A Westhampton meadow-and-upland name related linguistically to Appaquogue, with forms including Apaucuck, Appocock, and Apockac.
map_geometry_source: Approximate modern point for Beaverdam Creek, historically associated with Apocock/Apaucuck; not an exact historic coordinate.
why_this_matters: Apocock connects the Beaverdam Creek area to wetland plants, meadowland, and the practical materials of Native coastal life. Its interpretation as flaggy land or a covering-place points to reeds and other plants used for mats, shelters, and everyday work, while related records also place the creek within a broader Native territorial landscape. Wetlands were knowledgeable homelands shaped by language, ecology, and community use, not empty margins.
introduction_content: Apocock is identified as a Westhampton placename for a tract of upland and meadow east of Beaverdam Creek. The source records several spellings and notes that the locality was also called Paucuck. It is kept separate from the East Hampton Appaquogue place because the sources describe different locations.
translation_content:
Apocock is treated as a variation of Appaquogue and is interpreted as flaggy land or wigwam-covering place. Recorded forms include Apaucuck, Apocuck, Appocock, Apockac, and Apocock. The shared interpretation does not make this the same site as East Hampton Appaquogue. Pawcuck is also recorded as a Westhampton neck form cross-referenced to Apocuck.

Why Place Names Matter

“Indigenous place names have existed for thousands of years, reflecting deep connections to land, water, and community.”

— BC Geographical Names Office, BC Geographical Names Office (2026), Indigenous Tag section
whereintheworld_content: Apocock preserves a place name tied to land, water, plant materials, and Native boundary-making on the south shore. Similar Algonquian place-name forms need careful location review: related words can point to different places and histories.
